surveys.narrative: Trout Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large, deep, have irregular shoreline shapes, and have clear and soft (unmineralized) water. Trout Lake is typical of lakes in this lake class except that it is smaller (7,641 acres) than the lake class average of 29,503 acres.Trout Lake was thermally stratified on 7/29/2002 and retained 5 ppm oxygen to a depth of 80 ft where the temperature was 46 F, and retained 3 ppm oxygen to near the bottom. Trout Lake ranks as mesotrophic-to-oligotrophic according to Carlson's Trophic State Index using a Secchi water clarity of 4.9 m, Chlorophyll-a of 4.7 ppb, and total phosphorus of 11 ppb (the total phosphorus reading is from 1993, as the 2002 reading was lower than the detection limit of 20 ppb).The major inlet to Trout Lake is from Pine Lake and has a rapids at the inlet and a beaver dam upstream which may limit fish movement. The inlet from Little Trout Lake is navigable. Other inlets are seasonal drainages from local bogs. The outlet, to Lake Vermilion, has a steep, rocky rapids which limits fish movement. There is a known walleye spawning run in the narrows to Little Trout Lake which is heavily fished by anglers each spring.Lake bottom substrates along shore are mostly boulder, rubble, gravel, and ledge rock. Aquatic plants are sparse and grow to a depth of 12 ft. Most plants are in shallow protected bays; the most common plants are sweetgale and sedges along the shore fringe, and water lobelia, water horehound, and quillwort.Trout Lake is in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, administered by the La Croix Ranger District of the U.S. Forest Service. There are 44 campsites on the lake and camping is limited to these campsites. A BWCAW permit is required to visit Trout Lake; quotas are established, fees are assessed for overnight stays, and there is a fee to reserve a camping or motor use permit. Day-use non-motorized permits have no quotas or fees. Unreserved day motor use permits have no fee, but are subject to quotas. Outboard use is limited to 25 horsepower maximum and snowmobiles are prohibited. Most access to Trout Lake is by the truck portage from Lake Vermilion, where a concessionaire will pull boats to Trout Lake using ATV's and boat trailers. In 2002, the round-trip fee was about $20, depending on the size of the load. A canoe portage from Lake Vermilion along Trout Creek (36 rods) is also heavily used.Fish sampling in this fisheries lake survey consisted of trapnets, shoreline seines, shallow gillnets set in water warmer than 55 F in depths of 8 ft to 24 ft, and deep gillnets set in water colder than 55 F in depths of 50 ft to 89 ft. Previously, two fisheries lake surveys and six fish population assessments dating back to 1958 consisted of 7-20 deep gillnet sets. Shallow gillnets were used during five of these investigations and shoreline seines were used only during the two surveys. Trapnets were used for the first time in 2002. Quartile statistics have not been calculated for stratified deep and shallow gillnet sets and are not provided in this report.Shallow Water Fish Populations:Shallow water fish populations in 2002 were dominated by walleye, rock bass, and bluegill sunfish. Smallmouth bass and yellow perch were not abundant in sampling nets, but smallmouth were probably underrepresented in the net catches as they are known to be "net shy", and yellow perch were a common food item found in walleye stomachs. The total catch of fish (all species combined) in the shallow gillnets in 2002 of 32.5 fish/net (21.7 lb/net) was similar to the median catch of 29.2 fish/net (25.3 lb/net) in all investigations on this lake. Walleye numbers in 2002 (16.7/shallow gillnet) were similar to the median catch of 13.6/shallow gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Walleye sizes in 2002 averaged 11.7" (0.6 lb), which is smaller than the long term average size in this lake of 12.9". The largest walleye, caught in a deep gillnet, was 25.6". Strong walleye year classes present in 2002 (expressed as a percentage of walleye captured in all gear types) were: 20% age one (2001 year class); 17% age three (1999); and 35% age four (1998). Growth of walleye age one through five was slower than normal by area standards, while growth of walleye age six and older appeared to be faster than normal.Rock bass numbers in 2002 (9.7/shallow gillnet) were similar to the median catch of 8.8/shallow gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Rock bass numbers in the trapnets in 2002 (20.7/net) were in the fourth quartile for this lake class. Rock bass sizes averaged 5.3" in the trapnets and 6.3" in the shallow gillnets; the largest rock bass was 10.8".Bluegill numbers in 2002 (19.0/trapnet) were in the third quartile for this lake class. Bluegill sizes averaged 5.2"; the largest was 7.8". Sixty four percent of the bluegill were age three, and all bluegill were ages three through six. Bluegill growth was normal by area standards.Smallmouth bass were not reported as being present in the initial lake survey in 1958. Their numbers have gradually increased to their abundance in 2002 of 2.0/shallow gillnet. They were also present in the trapnets and shoreline seines, and were visually observed in the shallows by the survey crew. Smallmouth sizes in the shallow gillnets in 2002 averaged 11.9"; the largest was 16.7". Smallmouth growth was slightly faster than normal by area standards. Nine of 10 smallmouth examined were infected with bass tapeworm.Deep Water Fish Populations:Deep water fish populations in 2002 were dominated by cisco. Burbot numbers have been cyclical in this lake and were much lower in 2002 than in the past few assessments. Lake trout numbers remained low despite large stockings of yearling lake trout every other year. The total catch of fish (all species combined) in the deep gillnets in 2002 of 53.2 fish/net (19.0 lb/net) was similar to the median catch of 52.1 fish/net (25.5 lb/net) in all investigations on this lake.Cisco numbers in 2002 (49.5/deep gillnet) were similar to the median catch of 45.3/deep gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Cisco sizes in 2002 averaged 9.0", which was similar to their average size in previous investigations. The largest cisco in 2002 was 15.3". Forty five of 120 cisco examined were infected with triaenophorus and thirty seven were infected with bladderworm. Triaenophorus and bladderworm are common parasites to cisco that are native to the area and cannot infect humans.Burbot numbers in 2002 (0.4/deep gillnet) were lower than the median catch of 1.8/deep gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Burbot numbers in Trout Lake appeared to cycle between low numbers (an average of 0.6/deep gillnet in four investigations from 1969 through 1987 and 0.4/deep gillnet in 2002), and high numbers (5.0/deep gillnet) in 1958 and an average of 5.6/deep gillnet in three investigations from 1992 through 1998. Burbot sizes in 2002 averaged 15.6", which was smaller than the average size of 20.1" in all investigations on this lake. The largest burbot captured in 2002 was 17.0".Lake trout numbers in 2002 (0.6/deep gillnet) were at the median for all investigations on this lake. Lake trout catches have always been low in this lake except for a spike in the 1980's (1.6/deep gillnet in 1982 and 2.1/deep gillnet in 1987). Lake trout sizes in 2002 averaged 21.0", which was similar to the average size of 21.2" in all investigations on this lake. Two of the nine lake trout captured in 2002 were fin-clipped fish which had been stocked as yearlings in the spring of 2001 and had grown to an average size of 12.0" when recaptured 14 months later. Six trout were not clipped and ranged in age (based on otolith reading) from age four through age seven. Since all trout stocked in Trout Lake since 1990 have been fin-clipped, this indicates some natural reproduction has occurred. One large lake trout (32.6") was released alive. Lake trout growth was faster than normal by area standards. Stomachs of eight trout were examined: four were empty, four contained cisco and two of these also contained perch or sculpin.

This was a deep water population assessment. Only gill nets were set and all were below 55 F (40').Fish populations were dominated by very high numbers of cisco (60.3/gill net) and high numbers of burbot (9.1/gill net). Low numbers of lake trout (0.4/gill net) were also present.Cisco sizes ranged from 6" to 15" and averaged 9.8". Burbot ranged from 14" to 29" and averaged 19.7"Lake trout were aged using otoliths. Three smaller ones were immature males, ages 5 and 6, and ranged in size from 16" to 23". One mature male, age 12, was 28". One mature female, age 14, was also 28". Trout were eating cisco and sculpins.

Trout Lake is located approximately 7 miles NW of Tower and is entirely within the BWCAW. There is a 25 hp limit for outboard motor use and snowmobile use is prohibited. There are numerous USFS campsites surrounding this popular lake. Most visitors access the lake via a portage from Lake Vermilion where a concessionaire will transport your boat with an ATV and trailer to Trout Lake. Several other portages provide access to the lake from the surrounding area.

The 2014 special assessment was focused on the deepwater fish community. Of particular interest was the contribution of stocked yearling lake trout to the overall population of lake trout. Fish sampling in 2014 included cisco (98%) and lake trout (2%). Two yellow perch were sampled incidentally.

Lake trout numbers in 2014 (1.3/gill net) were higher than the long term average (0.7/gill net) for this lake. Trout sizes averaged 14.7 inches; smaller than the long term average (20.7 inches) for this lake. The largest lake trout sampled in 2014 was 31.5 inches long. Fourteen (67%) of the lake trout sampled were from stocking, eleven of which were recently stocked in the spring of 2014 and averaged only 8.0 inches long.

Cisco abundance in 2014 (60.2/gill net) was higher than the historic average (55.2/gill net). The average cisco sampled was 9.4 inches which is similar to past assessments (9.0 inches). The largest cisco sampled in 2014 was 16.5 inches long.

Trout Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large, very deep, have very irregular shoreline shapes, and have very clear and soft (unmineralized) water. Trout Lake is typical of lakes in this lake class, except that it is smaller (7,641 acres) than the lake class average of 29,503 acres.Trout Lake stratifies thermally in midsummer and in 1998 retained good oxygen (5 ppm) to a depth of 73 ft, where the temperature was 46 F. The major inlet, from Pine Lake, has a rocky rapids at Trout Lake which prevents upstream fish movement. The channel to Little Trout Lake is navigable by boats and fish. The outlet to Lake Vermilion has a rocky rapids which prevents upstream fish movement. Shallow water bottom substrates in Trout Lake are mostly boulder, sand, and ledgerock. Aquatic plants are very sparse and consist mostly of sedges, bulrush, sweetgale, narrowleaf pondweed, and floatingleaf pondweed.This special fish assessment consisted of 16 gillnets set in water colder than 55 F, at depths of 40 ft to 95 ft. The purpose was to assess cold water fish populations and to evaluate survival and growth of stocked lake trout. Six previous cold water fish assessments have been conducted on Trout Lake, in 1958, 1977, 1982, 1987, 1992, and 1993.The total catch of fish (all species combined) in Trout Lake in 1998 of 52 fish/gillnet (27 lb/gillnet) was very close to the average of 60 fish/gillnet (26 lb/gillnet) captured in the six previous cold water assessments on this lake. Cold water fish populations in 1998 were dominated by cisco and burbot. Low numbers of lake trout, walleye, and white sucker were also caught.Cisco numbers in 1998 (45.3/gillnet) were similar to the long term average catch of 55/gillnet in Trout Lake. Cisco populations have varied, ranging from 24/gillnet (1958 and 1977) to 94/gillnet (1992), but there appears to have been a general increase in cisco numbers over time in Trout Lake. Cisco sizes in 1998 were similar to previous assessments and averaged 9.5"; the largest cisco was 15.4". One 12" cisco had a yellow perch in its gut, which is unusual as cisco normally forage on invertebrates.Burbot numbers in 1998 (5.8/gillnet) were higher than the long term average catch of 2.9/gillnet. Burbot numbers in Trout Lake have generally been low, ranging from 0.3 to 1.8/gillnet, but were higher in 1958 (5.0/gillnet), in 1993 (9.1/gillnet) , and in this assessment. Burbot sizes in 1998 averaged 19.8"; the largest burbot was 25.4". Burbot were foraging on cisco, and had "mouthed" the scales off the majority of the cisco captured in the gillnets.Lake trout numbers in 1998 (0.2/gillnet) were lower than the long term average catch of 1.2/gillnet. The highest trout numbers (average of 1.8/gillnet) occurred from 1977 through 1987, a period of intensive lake trout stocking, and also a period when cisco and burbot numbers were much lower than at present. Of the three lake trout captured in 1998, one had a clipped fin indicating it was a survivor of the 1995 stocking of 37,000 lake trout yearlings. Other recent trout stockings (34,000 yearlings in 1997, 75,000 fingerlings in 1992, and 76,000 fingerlings in 1990) were not represented in the 1998 gillnetting catch. Two of the captured trout had cisco in their guts, the third had yellow perch in its gut. The three lake trout were captured at depths of 54 ft to 78 ft.

Trout Lake is located approximately 9 miles NW of Tower and is entirely within the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. A 25 hp maximum outboard motor restriction is present. With a surface area of 9,237 acres and maximum depth of 90 ft, it is similar to other lakes in the area such as Basswood and Burntside.

Trout Lake has a long history of lake trout stocking and recent findings indicate that natural reproduction continues to be present. For this special assessment we targeted suspected spawning areas for the purpose of collecting DNA for genetic ancestry testing.

A total of 54 lake trout (0.96/net) were sampled using 3/4" double pot trap nets. Only one lake trout was fin clipped which indicates a stocked individual. The remaining 53 lake trout were unclipped. Only two females were sampled. The average length of lake trout sampled was 26.8" and the largest was 37.4" long.

Temperature and dissolved oxygen measurements were collected from the deepest basin in Trout Lake on August 5th, 2025. This was done to evaluate the quantity and quality of cold, oxygenated water (i.e., oxythermal habitat) available to Lake Trout, the most sensitive coldwater species present in this lake (Cisco, also known as 'Tullibee', are also present). Lake Trout require a layer of oxythermal habitat that contains water temperatures below 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) and dissolved oxygen concentrations above 3.0 mg/L. Based on data collected from the deepest basin (maximum sampled depth was 85.3 feet), the water temperature decreased to 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) at 59.0 feet and the dissolved oxygen concentration stayed greater than 3.0 mg/L for the entire sampled depth. This layer in the water column was 26.2 feet, indicating oxythermal habitat for Lake Trout was present.
Further, the temperature at which dissolved oxygen decreased to 3.0 mg/L (i.e., TDO3, a single variable to characterize oxythermal habitat) was never reached because dissolved oxygen remained above 3.0 mg/L throughout the sampled depths. In this case, the minimum temperature, 7.9 degrees C (46.2 degrees F), was substituted as TDO3. TDO3 values cooler than 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) indicate that oxythermal conditions were suitable for Lake Trout at the time of the survey.
Data collected by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources during the period of maximum oxythermal stress (July 26th to Aug 24th) in 4 years during 2006-2023 indicated unsuitable oxythermal habitat in most years surveyed, with unfavorable conditions recorded in 2006, 2008, 2010 when there was no suitable oxythermal habitat layer. When adequate oxythermal habitat is not available, Lake Trout are squeezed into unfavorable, warmer water conditions and experience higher levels of stress. Despite the low values for oxythermal habitat since 2006, the latest three fisheries surveys, in 2014, 2018, and 2022, caught moderate numbers of Lake Trout in deewater nets.

Trout Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large, deep, have irregular shoreline shapes, and have clear and soft (unmineralized) water. Trout Lake is smaller than most of the lakes in this lake class.

Trout Lake was thermally stratified on 07/31/2006 with a surface temperature about 74 F and a bottom temperature about 50 F. Adequate oxygen for lake trout (more than 5 ppm) was retained to within about 10 feet of the bottom, where the temperature was about 50 F.

The major inlet to Trout Lake is from Pine Lake and has rapids and beaver dams that limit fish movement. The outlet, to Lake Vermilion, has a steep, rocky rapids that limits fish movement. Walleye spawn near the narrows to Little Trout Lake each spring, and this is a popular fishing spot during the fishing opener in early May. Lake bottom substrates along the shoreline are mostly boulder, rubble, gravel, and ledge rock. Aquatic plants are sparse and grow to a depth of 12 feet. Most are found in shallow bays.

Trout Lake is in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. There are 44 campsites on the lake. Motorboats (25 horsepower maximum) are allowed, but snowmobiles are not. Visitor use requires a permit and is subject to quotas. Contact the U.S. Forest Service Lac La Croix Ranger District (218) 666-0020 for details.

Fish sampling in this assessment was for determining the survival and growth of the Gillis Lake and Mountain Lake strains of lake trout yearings that have been stocked biennially (in odd years) at the rate of 38,000 for each stocking (5.0 yearlings per surface acre). All of these stocked trout had clipped fins (adipose, left or right ventral, depending on the strain and year stocked) so they could be identified at recapture. Also of interest was identifying young, unclipped trout that would indicate natural reproduction by lake trout, and monitoring populations of cisco and burbot.

Sixteen gillnets were set in or below the thermocline in 2006, at depths of 40 to 87 feet. Ten previous coldwater investigations on Trout Lake, dating back to 1958, used 7-20 deep gillnets to assess coldwater fish populations.

The lake trout catch in 2006 of 0.8/deep gillnet was similar to the median catch of 0.6/deep gillnet in Trout Lake. Lake trout catches in this lake have ranged from 0.1/deep gillnet in 1969 to 2.1/deep gillnet in 1987.

Twelve lake trout were captured in the 2006 assessment. Four of these trout had left ventral fin clips indicating they were Gillis Lake strain that had been stocked as yearlings averaging 6.5 inches in the spring of 2003, and had grown to an average size of 20.2 inches (range: 18.2 to 22.6 inches) when recaptured at the age of 4. One small lake trout had a left ventral fin clip indicating it was Mountain Lake strain from a yearling stocking in spring 2005 that averaged 6.4 inches and had grown to 8.9 inches when captured at age 2.

Seven lake trout had no fin clips, indicating they were likely naturally produced (clipped fins sometimes regenerate if they are not completely removed). Six of these unclipped trout were aged using otoliths. Growth of the age four unclipped trout averaged 15.0 inches (range: 14.4 to 15.6 inches), which was smaller than the average length of 20.2 inches for the clipped age four trout. The stocked trout may be faster growing than naturally produced trout in this lake, or they may have had an additional growth advantage in their first year in the hatchery that they never relinquished. Trout stomach contents were not examined in 2006.

Burbot numbers in 2006 (0.1/deep gillnet) were the lowest of any investigation on Trout Lake. Burbot catches in Trout Lake have cycled between low numbers (an average of 0.6/deep gillnet in four investigations from 1969 through 1987 and an average of 0.3/deep gillnet in three investigations from 2002 through 2006) and high numbers (5.0/deep gillnet in 1958 and an average of 5.6/deep gillnet in three investigations from 1992 through 1998). High numbers of burbot appear to be associated with low numbers of lake trout in this lake, and it is hoped that the low numbers of burbot in recent investigations combined with intensive lake trout yearling stocking will allow lake trout numbers to rebound. The average size of burbot has gradually declined over time in Trout Lake, from about 21 inches in early investigations to about 14 inches in recent investigations.

Cisco numbers in 2006 (50/deep gillnet) were similar to the median catch of 49/deep gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Cisco sizes in 2006 averaged 8.8 inches, which was similar to the average size of 8.9 inches in all investigations on this lake. Cisco were not examined for parasites in 2006, but previous investigations have shown that many are infected with bladder roundworm and triaenophorus.

Trout Lake is located approximately 7 miles NW of Tower and is entirely within the BWCAW. Outboard motors up to a maximum of 25 hp are allowed. Snowmobile use is prohibited. Other BWCAW rules and regulations apply when visiting this lake.

The most common access is via 1/2 mile portage from Lake Vermilion where a concessionaire will transport your watercraft by ATV and trailer to Trout Lake. There are several other portages surrounding the lake for addtional access options. Designated USFS campsites are common around the lake for overnight and day use.

The 2018 survey of Trout Lake was focused on the deepwater fish community, in particular the survival of stocked lake trout. Twenty-seven lake trout were sampled in 2018 and cisco dominated the catch (94%). Northern pike, smallmouth bass and walleye were incidentally sampled in low relative abundances.

Lake trout numbers in 2018 (1.5/gill net) were slightly above the historical average (0.8/gill net) for this lake. Eight stocked trout were sampled and all but one of them were under 9 inches long and from stocking in the prior spring. The only other stocked lake trout sampled was 19.5 inches. As we have seen in previous surveys, the stocked lake trout rarely acheive large size indicating that their survival is poor.

Naturally reproduced lake trout ranged from 12 to 28 inches long. Overall, the lake trout average length was 15 inches which is smaller than the historic average length of 21 inches. This average was lowered by the number of small stocked fish in 2018, which typically were not caught in past surveys. Fin-clipped yearling lake trout were stocked in even years in Trout Lake through 2018.

Cisco are an important forage fish for lake trout. Numbers in 2018 (37.3/gill net) were below the historic average (50.4/gill net). Cisco average length was 9.3 inches which is slightly larger than the historic average length of 8.9 inches. Cisco sizes ranged from 5.4 inches up to 17.4 inches.

Trout Lake is located nine miles north of Tower and just north of Lake Vermilion but is entirely within the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness (BWCAW). It has a number of portages to nearby lakes, but the main lake access is via a motor portage from Lake Vermilion. The lake is 7,425 acres and although it is entirely within the BWCAW, 25 hp and under outboards are permitted. Motor use permits are required from the US Forest Service. The lake has a maximum depth of 98 feet and clear water. There are several small to moderate sized inlets mostly on the lakes east and north sides. Only one outlet exists which flows out the southernmost point and into Lake Vermilion. Trout Lake is a prototypical northern Minnesota/Canadian shield water body with shorelines covered in tall pines, areas of granite ledge rock, and exceptionally clear water. Lake bottom substrates along the shoreline are mostly boulder and ledgerock with some areas of rubble and cobble. A few bays have soft bottoms but vegetation is fairly sparse. Additionally, a few bays are quite sandy and make for great swimming areas. On July 17, 2022, the dissolved oxygen profile showed thermal stratification with a surface temperature of 74 F and bottom temperature 46 F. The water temperatures suitable for lake trout were reached around 33 feet. Oxygen levels suitable for lake trout were sustained throughout the water column. The overall deep water gillnet catch rate for all fish combined was 39.3 fish/net which was below average for the lake. Yield was 21.0 lbs/net which was right at the lake's historic average. Fish species sampled in deep water gill nets were cisco, lake trout, and walleye. The overall shallow water gillnet catch rate for all fish combined was 10.8 fish/net which was the lowest on record for the lake. Yield was 16.3 lbs/net which was also the lowest on record for the lake. Fish species sampled were rock bass, walleye, northern pike, yellow perch, white sucker, smallmouth bass, bluegill, and pumpkinseed. The deep water gillnet catch for lake trout in 2022 was 1.3 fish/net which was better than the average for past surveys of Trout Lake. Lengths ranged from 13 to over 33 inches with an average of just over 25 inches. The average weight was very impressive at nearly 6.5 lbs/fish. Of the fish that were aged, ages ranged from 4 to 19 years. Lake trout growth was fairly fast with the average fish taking 8 years to reach 22 inches long. Six-hundred-eighty-one cisco were caught in deep water gill nets for a catch rate of 37.8 fish/net. This was below average compared to past surveys on Trout Lake but still quite good when compared to other cisco lakes in the Tower area. Sizes were 6.5 to nearly 16 inches with an average of just over 9 inches. Sizes appear to have remained fairly consistent throughout the years. Thirty-seven walleye were sampled in the shallow water gill nets for a catch rate of 3.1 fish/net. This catch rate was the lowest on record for Trout Lake. Lengths ranged from 8.5 to just over 24 inches with an average of nearly 19 inches. Average weight was 2.5 pounds. Growth rates were quite good when compared to other similar lakes and other walleye populations in the Tower area. Ages ranged from 1 to 23 years old with the strongest year class coming in 2017. The northern pike shallow water gillnet catch was 1.3 fish/net which was on par with previous surveys of Trout Lake. Lengths ranged from 20.5 to just over 35 inches with an average of 25.5 inches. Sizes were similar to previous surveys. The average weight was nearly four pounds. Eight smallmouth bass were sampled in shallow water gill nets for a catch rate of 0.7 fish/net which was the lowest catch rate on record since smallmouth were first sampled in 1977. The average weight was just over a pound per fish. Lengths ranged from 11 to just over 16 inches with an average of just over 13 inches. Growth was somewhat slow compared to other smallmouth lakes in the area. The average smallmouth was eight inches long at four years old. Ages ranged from 4 to 12 years.

The Secchi water clarity on 7/26/2004 was 16 ft and the total alkalinity was 7.0 ppm. These are similar to measurements taken on Trout Lake in previous investigations. The surface temperature on 07/26/2004 was 71 F and the bottom temperature was 48 F. The thermocline was very gradual, beginning at 21 ft and extending to 52 ft, where the temperature was 51 F. Good oxygen for trout (more than 6 ppm) was retained to within 10 ft of the bottom at both of the sampling stations in Trout lake. Oxygen levels at the bottom were 4 ppm. Fish sampling in this special deep water fish assessment was for determining the survival and growth of the Gillis Lake strain of lake trout yearlings which have been stocked biennially (in odd years) in Trout Lake at the rate of 38,000 per stocking (5.0 per acre) since 1995. All of these stocked trout had clipped fins (adipose, left ventral, or right ventral, depending on the year) so they could be identified at recapture. Also of interest were young unclipped trout that would indicate natural reproduction of the remnant lake trout population in the lake, and populations of cisco and burbot.Sixteen standard gillnets were set in or below the thermocline in 2004 at depths of 42 ft to 91 ft. Nine previous deep water investigations dating back to 1958 have been conducted on Trout Lake, using 7-20 deep gillnets.Four lake trout were captured in 2004. Three of these trout, all with fin clips, were in one net just southwest of the southern tip of Sioux Pine Island. One unclipped trout was captured in a net just southeast of the southern tip of Sioux Pine Island. Lake trout catches in Trout Lake have historically been low, with a median catch of 0.6 trout/deep gillnet. The 2004 catch of 0.25 trout/deep gillnet ties with the 1998 assessment for the lowest lake trout catch in any investigation on Trout Lake except for a 1969 research study in which many of the gillnets were set in water too shallow for trout. This result is a disappointment because a recent decline in previously abundant burbot numbers led us to hope that stocked trout survival might be better than in the past.The smallest trout captured in 2004 was 12.6" with a left ventral fin clip and had been stocked as a yearling in the spring of 2003. A 13.6" unclipped trout, apparently the result of natural reproduction, was aged at three years by its otolith. The two largest trout, 20.9" and 21.1", were right ventral clipped fish which had been stocked as yearlings in the spring of 2001. Two of the lake trout had cisco in their stomachs; the remaining two had empty stomachs.Burbot numbers in 2004 (0.25/deep gillnet) were the lowest of any investigation on Trout Lake. Burbot numbers in Trout Lake appear to cycle between low numbers (an average of 0.6/deep gillnet in four investigations from 1969 through 1987 and an average of 0.4/deep gillnet in 2002 and 2004) and high numbers (5.0/deep gillnet in 1958 and an average of 5.6/deep gillnet in three investigations from 1992 through 1998). Burbot sizes in 2004 averaged 14.5", which was smaller than the average size of 19.6" in all investigations on this lake. The largest burbot captured in 2004 was 15.2".Cisco numbers in 2004 (69.0/deep gillnet) were higher than the median catch of 47.4/deep gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Cisco sizes in 2004 averaged 8.1", which is similar to the average length of 8.9" in all investigations on this lake. The largest cisco captured in 2004 was 18.4", which was the largest ever caught in this lake. Cisco were not examined for parasites in 2004, but previous investigations have shown than many are infected with bladder roundworm and triaenophorus.

Trout Lake is in Ecological Lake Class 2, which consists of 15 lakes in northeast Minnesota that are very large, deep, have irregular shoreline shapes, and have clear and soft (unmineralized) water. Trout Lake is smaller than most of the lakes in this lake class.

Trout Lake was thermally stratified on 7/28/2008 with surface temperatures of 70 F and bottom temperatures of 47 F. Adequate oxygen for trout (more than 5 ppm) was retained to a depth of 82 ft where the temperature was 47 F, and adequate oxygen for warmer water fish species (more than 2 ppm) was retained to the bottom, where there was 3.6 ppm oxygen. Trout Lake ranks as mestrophic-to-oligotrophic according to Carlson's Trophic State Index.

The major inlet to Trout Lake is from Pine Lake and has rapids at the inlet and a beaver dam upstream, both of which limit fish movement. The inlet from Little Trout Lake is navigable at high water and shallow at low water. Other inlets are seasonal drainages from local bogs. The outlet, to Lake Vermilion, has a steep rocky rapids which limits fish movement. There is a known walleye spawning run in the narrows to Little Trout Lake, which is heavily fished by anglers each spring.

Lake bottom substrates along the shoreline of Trout Lake are mostly boulder, rubble, gravel, and ledgerock. Aquatic plants are sparse and grow to a depth of 12 ft. Most plants are in shallow protected bays; the most common plants are sweetgale and sedges along the shore fringe, and water lobelia, water horehound, and quillwort.

Trout Lake is in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, administered by the La Croix Ranger District of the U.S. Forest Service. There are 44 campsites on the lake and camping is limited to these campsites. A BWCAW permit is required to visit Trout Lake; quotas are established, fees are assessed for overnight stays, and there is a fee to reserve camping or motor use permits. Day-use non-motorized permits have no quotas or fees. Unreserved day motor use permits have no fee, but are subject to quotas. Outboard use is limited to 25 horsepower maximum and snowmobiles are prohibited. Most access to Trout Lake is by the truck portage from Lake Vermilion, where a concessionaire will pull boats to Trout Lake using an ATV and boat trailer. In 2008, the round-trip fee was about $30, depending on the size of the load. A canoe portage from Lake Vermilion along Trout Creek (36 rods) is also heavily used.

Fish sampling in the 2008 fish population assessment was done with shallow gillnets set in water warmer than 55 F in depths of 8 ft to 23 ft, and deep gillnets set in water colder than 55 F in depths of 42 ft to 87 ft. Previously, three fisheries lake surveys and eight fish population assessments dating back to 1958 consisted of 7-20 deep gillnet sets. Shallow gillnets (4-8 sets) were used during six of these investigations, and shoreline seines were used only during the three surveys. Trapnets were used for the first time in 2002. Quartile statistics for comparing gillnet catches in Trout Lake to other lakes in this lake class have not been calculated for stratified shallow and deep gillnet sets, so are not provided in this report.

SHALLOW WATER FISH POPULATIONS:
Shallow water fish populations in 2008 were dominated by walleye and rock bass. Bluegill sunfish were abundant in the trapnets in 2002, but they are not sampled well with gillnets and so are probably more abundant than indicated in the 2008 investigation where no trapnets were used. Smallmouth bass numbers appear to be increasing, plus bass are "net-shy" and difficult to catch in standard sampling nets, so their numbers were probably underrepresented in the net catches. Yellow perch numbers were low in the shallow gillnets in 2008, but small yellow perch were the most common food item found in walleye stomachs, so perch numbers may be higher than indicated by the gillnet catch. The total catch of fish (all species combined) in the shallow gillnets in 2008 of 38.8 fish/net (30.9 lb/net) was similar to the median catch of 31.0 fish/net (27.4 lb/net) in all investigations on this lake.

Walleye numbers in 2008 (18.5/shallow gillnet) were high when compared to most area lakes, but were similar to the median catch of 15.0/shallow gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Walleye sizes in 2008 averaged 13.8" (1.1 lb), which was similar to the long-term average size in this lake of 13.1". The largest walleye was 26.3". The strongest year-class was from 2005 and comprised 47 percent of all walleye caught in 2008. Growth of walleye age 1-5 was somewhat slower than normal (in the second quartile) by area standards, while growth of walleye age 6 and older appeared to be faster than normal.

Rock bass numbers in 2008 (14.5/shallow gillnet) were higher than the median catch of 9.7/shallow gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Rock bass sizes averaged 6.1"; the largest rock bass was 8.1"

Smallmouth bass were not reported as being present in the initial lake survey in 1958. Their numbers have gradually increased to their abundance in 2008 of 3.0/shallow gillnet. In 2002 they were also present in the trapnets and shoreline seines, and were visually observed in the shallows by the survey crew. Smallmouth bass sizes in 2008 averaged 10.4"; the largest was 14.6". Smallmouth growth was normal by area standards.

A few of the shallow water game fish examined in 2008 were infected with neascus (black spot). Most of the smallmouth bass also were infected with bass tapeworm larvae in their viscera.

DEEP WATER FISH POPULATIONS
Deep water fish sampling was done in 2008 to evaluate the survival and growth of lake trout yearlings which have been stocked biennially (in odd years) in Trout Lake at the rate of 38,000 per stocking (5.0 per acre) since 1995. Gillis Lake strain yearlings were stocked from 1995 through 2003 and Mountain Lake strain yearlings were stocked in 2005 and 2007. All of these stocked trout had clipped fins (adipose, left ventral, right ventral, or a combination of the adipose and one of the ventral fins, depending on the year) so they could be identified at recapture. Also of interest were young unclipped trout that would indicate natural reproduction of the remnant lake trout population in the lake, and populations of cisco and burbot.

Lake trout numbers in 2008 (1.1/deep gillnet) were higher than the median lake trout catch of 0.7/deep gillnet in all investigations on this lake, but were lower than the median catch of 2.2/deep gillnet in recent investigations on 33 lake trout lakes in the Tower Fisheries Management Area. Many of the stomachs of lake trout captured in 2008 contained cisco, although sculpins and sticklebacks were also found.

Eighteen lake trout were captured in 2008. Seven of these trout had clipped fins (all were left pelvic fin-clips), indicating they had been stocked. Comparison with the stocking record and previous catches of fin-clipped trout indicates that three of these trout, averaging 19.1", were likely age four from the 2005 stocking of Mountain Lake strain yearlings. The remaining four clipped trout, averaging 24.5", were likely age six from the 2003 stocking of Gillis Lake strain yearlings. No otoliths were taken from fin clipped trout in 2008.

Ageing of the ten unclipped trout from which otolith samples were taken proved to be problematic, as growth of these fish appeared to be much slower than growth of the clipped fish. For example, two unclipped trout, averaging 16.5", were aged at 6 years, while four unclipped trout averaging 19.4" were aged at 8-10 years.

While stocked yearling trout should have somewhat better growth because their first year was in a hatchery instead of the wild, the observed discrepancy this year seems too large. It should be noted that the fin-clipping regime was recently changed to accommodate a comparison of Gillis Lake and Mountain Lake strains, and as a result two consecutive stockings of left pelvic clips were done (in 2003 - Gillis Lake strain, and 2005 - Mountain Lake strain). In the future, identical clips will separate stocked lake trout by four years instead of the six years originally planned. Also, the person that had read our lake trout otoliths retired and a new person began reading otoliths this year by cracking and burning one otolith of each pair and sending the matching otolith to Paul Hauck, who has much experience and training in reading lake trout otoliths. These two readings for each fish matched remarkably well, although Paul said they were very dense and difficult to read. In the future, otoliths should be taken both from unclipped trout and from fin-clipped trout to try to resolve the apparent discrepancy in their ages.

Burbot numbers in 2008 (0.2/deep gillnet) were lower than the median burbot catch of 0.8/deep gillnet in all investigations on this lake, and continues a trend of low burbot numbers following very high burbot catches in the 1990's. Burbot numbers in Trout Lake have cycled between low numbers (an average of 0.6/deep gillnet in four investigations from 1969 through 1987 and an average of 0.2/deep gillnet in four investigations from 2002 through 2008) and high numbers (5.0/deep gillnet in 1958 and an average of 5.6/deep gillnet in three investigations from 1992 through 1998). Burbot sizes in 2008 averaged 17.7", which was similar to the average size of 18.9" in all investigations on this lake. The largest burbot captured in 2008 was 18.7".

Cisco numbers in 2008 (70.7/deep gillnet) were higher than the median catch of 49.9/deep gillnet in all investigations on this lake. Cisco sizes in 2008 averaged 9.0", which is similar to the average length of 8.9" in all investigations on this lake. The largest cisco captured in 2008 was 17.7". Cisco were not examined for parasites in 2008, but previous investigations have shown that many are infected with bladder roundworm and triaenophorus.

All of the parasites found on game fish in 2008 are native to the area and are common. They cannot infect humans, are often removed by filleting, and are killed at temperatures used to cook fish.

Angler reports in the last few years indicate that the lake trout population, which had been low and consisted mostly of a few large fish, is recovering. More small trout, both naturally produced and fin-clipped (stocked) are being caught. Fewer burbot have been reported by anglers in recent years.

Trout Lake is located approximately 7 miles NW of Tower, MN. It is entirely within the BWCAW and a USFS permit is required to access the lake. There is a 25 hp maximum limit for outboard motors and snowmobile use is prohibited. Most visitors access Trout Lake via the truck portage from Lake Vermilion where a concessionaire will transport watercraft with an ATV and trailer. There are several other carry in accesses present.

Trout Lake was thermally stratified on 07/30/2010 with a surface temperature of 72 F and a bottom (90 ft) temperature of 48.6 F. Dissolved oxygen exceeding 2 ppm was present to a depth of 90 ft.

Fish sampling during the 2010 special assessment focused on the deepwater fish community. A plankton sample was taken to determine the presence of spiny water flea. None were observed.

Lake trout numbers in 2010 (0.6/gill net) were identical to the long term average for all investigations on this lake. Lake trout sizes averaged 23.9 inches which was larger than the long term average of 21.1 inches for all investigations on this lake. The largest lake trout was 33 inches.

Burbot numbers in 2010 (0.3/gill net) were lower than the long term average of 0.7/gill net for all investigations on this lake. Burbot sizes averaged 20.5 inches which was larger than the long term average of 19.0 inches for all investigations on this lake. The largest burbot was 23 inches.

Cisco numbers in 2010 (77.2/gill net) were higher than the long term average of 50.2/gill net for all investigations on this lake. Cisco sizes averaged 9.9 inches which was larger than the long term average of 8.9 inches for all investigations on this lake. The largest cisco was 15 inches.

Several walleye and one smallmouth bass were also sampled. It is not unusual for these species to inhabit the deepwater areas while foraging.
